summary: This document defines a binding of XMPP over a WebSocket transport. This provides higher performance than the existing HTTP binding for XMPP.

eli5.summary: Chat apps need a fast, always-open line. WebSocket is a line that stays open in the browser, and this RFC explains how to run chat through it.

questions: how does xmpp work over websocket
what is the xmpp websocket subprotocol
how do browsers discover an xmpp websocket endpoint
subtitle: How browser-based chat clients can speak XMPP over a WebSocket instead of HTTP long polling.

tldr.problem: Browser XMPP clients had to tunnel through HTTP long polling (BOSH), which has high transport overhead, because browser APIs did not allow XMPP to run directly over TCP.
tldr.mechanism: The xmpp WebSocket subprotocol is negotiated in the WebSocket handshake. Each XMPP stanza or stream element is sent as its own text message, and new open and close elements replace the stream start and end tags.
tldr.outcome: Browser apps get a lower-overhead binding than the HTTP one, with TLS provided by wss and endpoints discovered through host-meta. It is a Proposed Standard with no replacement listed.

today: RFC 7395 is a Proposed Standard published in October 2014, and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why XMPP Needs a WebSocket Binding
sections.content:
Web applications that used XMPP relied on Bidirectional-streams Over Synchronous HTTP (BOSH), an XMPP binding to HTTP. BOSH uses HTTP long polling, so it suffers from high transport overhead compared with XMPP's native TCP binding, plus other long-polling problems described in RFC 6202.

Using XMPP directly would be better, but the APIs and sandbox in browsers do not allow it. The WebSocket protocol (RFC 6455) is bidirectional and has a simple message-based framing layer, so this RFC defines a WebSocket subprotocol for XMPP. It is designed for browser-based clients, which reach the same roster and contacts as TCP clients. The main difference is the transport binding.
sections.eli5: Instead of knocking on the server's door again and again, the web page opens a door that stays open for both sides to talk through.

sections.title: Handshake and Message Types
sections.content:
The client and server agree on the subprotocol during the WebSocket handshake. The client MUST list xmpp in its Sec-WebSocket-Protocol header, and the server's reply MUST include xmpp too. If the response lacks it, no XMPP connection exists and the client MUST close the WebSocket connection.

After the handshake, data frame messages MUST be of the text type and carry UTF-8 encoded data.
sections.eli5: Both sides say the secret word 'xmpp' when they meet. If the other side does not say it back, the client hangs up.

sections.title: Framing XMPP in WebSocket Messages
sections.content:
The WebSocket binding uses WebSocket's own messages to mark where things start and end, instead of one long streaming XML document. A framed stream begins with an <open/> element and ends with a <close/> element, both qualified by the namespace urn:ietf:params:xml:ns:xmpp-framing. They carry the same attributes as the <stream/> element in RFC 6120. A wrong namespace makes the receiver close the stream with an <invalid-namespace> error. There is no wrapping <stream:stream/> element.

Each frame corresponds to one WebSocket message and MUST be parsable as a standalone XML document, with its own namespace and language declarations. XML declarations are NOT RECOMMENDED, since messages are already UTF-8. The first character of each frame MUST be <, and every stanza or top-level element MUST be sent in its own frame. Stream features and errors must declare the stream prefix or use an unprefixed form, because no parent element supplies it.
sections.eli5: Each WebSocket message is one complete letter in its own envelope, so the reader never has to wait for a long scroll to finish.

sections.title: Opening, Restarting and Closing Streams
sections.content:
The first message after the handshake MUST be an <open/> from the initiating entity. The receiver MUST answer with an <open/> or a <close/>. Clients MUST NOT multiplex XMPP streams over the same WebSocket. Stream-level errors are fatal: the server sends the error as a complete element in a message, and if the error happens while opening, it sends its <open/> response first and the error in a second message, then closes.

To close, the closing party first sends <close/>. The stream is closed when the other side's <close/> arrives, and then the WebSocket closing handshake MUST be started. A connection broken without a stream close ends the session, though a server SHOULD keep a session alive for a while if stream management resumption was negotiated. A server may also send <close/> with a see-other-uri attribute to move the client to another endpoint, but clients MUST NOT accept an endpoint with a lower security context, such as going from wss:// to ws://.

When a stream restart is required, such as after SASL succeeds, both streams are implicitly closed. The client MUST send a new <open/> and MUST NOT send a <close/>.
sections.eli5: You say hello with 'open' and goodbye with 'close'. If the server says 'try the other door', you only go if that door is at least as safe.

sections.title: Keepalives, TLS and Stream Management
sections.content:
Whitespace keepalives MUST NOT be used, because every message must start with <. Instead, XMPP Ping (XEP-0199) or Stream Management (XEP-0198) MAY be used, and WebSocket ping frames MAY be used too, though browsers may not expose them.

TLS cannot run at the XMPP layer because the subprotocol does not allow raw binary data. When TLS is used it MUST be enabled at the WebSocket layer through the wss URI scheme. A server MUST NOT advertise TLS as a stream feature, and a client MUST ignore one if advertised. A client MAY use Stream Management to confirm delivery and to resume session state after a temporary network loss or after navigating to a new URL in a browser.
sections.eli5: Locks go on the whole road (wss), not on each parcel. To check the line is alive, use polite 'are you there?' messages, not silent blank ones.

sections.title: Discovering the WebSocket Endpoint
sections.content:
Browsers usually cannot read DNS SRV records, which the TCP binding uses for discovery. This RFC uses Web Host Metadata (RFC 6415) and Web Linking (RFC 5988) with the link relation urn:xmpp:alt-connections:websocket instead.

The client requests /.well-known/host-meta over secure HTTP at an origin matching the XMPP service domain, then reads a link of that relation, such as wss://im.example.org:443/ws. Servers MAY publish this and clients MAY use it. If the service domain differs from the endpoint's web origin, as in multi-tenant hosting, the host-meta document SHOULD be used to establish trust, as long as it was fetched over secure HTTP.
sections.eli5: The browser cannot look up the chat server in the phone book, so it asks the website's own sign: 'which door do I use for chat?'

sections.title: Security Considerations and IANA
sections.content:
The RFC lists how this binding differs from TCP. Discovery uses host-meta over HTTPS instead of DNS SRV, which it calls functionally equivalent. The authenticated identity is the connection endpoint address rather than the XMPP service domain, with delegation shown by host-meta. Framing has no effect on security properties, and in all other respects the security considerations of RFC 6120 apply.

Operators need to serve host-meta over https only, use wss only, and deploy certificates for both. Browser apps cannot inspect the certificate themselves and must trust the browser, which can only check it against the web origin. The downgrade rule for see-other-uri prevents moves from wss:// to ws://.

IANA registered the xmpp WebSocket subprotocol and the URN sub-namespace urn:ietf:params:xml:ns:xmpp-framing.
sections.eli5: Only use the locked, secure doors, and never let anyone talk you into moving to an unlocked one.
